The creator reported more than 1,700 players, 58 countries, and 158 Sustainable City completions after the first three days. Forty-two days later, the v1.0 report said almost 4,000 players in 77 countries and more than 137,000 power plants built. That is roughly 2.35× growth between rounded snapshots, with an average near 55 additional players per day after the initial launch spike.

Counterpoint. These are creator-reported totals, not an independent analytics audit. The initial >567 players/day launch burst and the later ~55/day average should not be described as one constant trajectory. Post reactions are engagement with different posts, not a time series for game users.
Play Grid Townlaunch reportv1.0 reportdeveloper site

The product promise is a planning problem, not a builder fantasy

The town grows automatically, but electricity does not. Homes, shops, factories, and data centres create changing hourly demand. The player buys generation and storage, connects buildings through a limited-reach grid, watches the day/night load curve, and tries to keep every home powered while the treasury and pollution cap remain viable. The final objective—Sustainable City—asks the player to reach 50 powered homes, keep homes lit through the night, stop burning gas, cover the peak with always-on generation or charged storage, and hold the fully clean state for 90 seconds. Hitting the pollution cap ends the run; the rules also warn that a negative balance can do the same.

1Read current demand and tonight's forecast
2Place generation or storage where it can connect
3Advance time and absorb town growth
4Review the dawn report and failure causes
5Draft an upgrade and revise the grid

Generation portfolio observed: Solar is cheap and clean but midday-only; Wind is variable and fades toward evening; Gas is available at any hour but adds fuel cost and pollution; Batteries move midday surplus into the peak; Hydro is clean and firm but restricted to river sites; Nuclear is costly, always-on capacity for later play.

Spatial rules matter. Each source has reach, wires cost upkeep, and some locations perform better than others. The placement overlay forecasts whether a site is valid and how close it is to ideal. New houses can grow beyond the existing network, so capacity and connection are separate problems.

Controls observed: mouse selection and placement; number keys 1–6 for sources; Inspect and Demolish modes; Space/pause; 1×, 2×, and 3× simulation speeds; zoom, pan, and camera rotation.

The first-session path

00:00–01:03

Analytics consent, five-part main menu, settings, stats, mode selection, Today's Grid briefing, How to Play, then the guided intro.

01:03–02:46

The guided shift starts with one unpowered farmhouse. It teaches a first Solar plant, the yellow site-quality overlay, network reach, the white demand line, the coloured generation curve, a second panel, and the 19:00 dinner peak. The interface explicitly notes that building does not pause time.

02:46–04:52

Inspect mode, Battery and Gas are introduced. Midday surplus charges storage; solar stops at sunset; the battery bridges part of the peak; Gas restores dark homes but turns fuel spend and pollution into visible running costs.

04:52–06:41

The simulation becomes less scripted: homes grow, income rises, a factory opens, Hydro is placed on a legal river site, and the first dawn report grades the grid.

06:41–09:18

A Grid Upgrade is chosen, camera and 3× speed are tested, more homes and factories appear, and a later upgrade changes the next planning cycle.

09:18–11:53

The Sustainable City meter rises while projected evening shortfalls keep widening. The town reaches a much denser state, but gas remains part of the mix.

11:53–12:25

Another upgrade decision arrives. Soon after, accumulated emissions hit the pollution cap on Day 5 and the run ends with 45 homes at peak and 58% clean energy.

Why the learning loop works

Context replaces a rules dump

The guided intro waits until a concept matters, pauses time, highlights one control, and gives a concrete next goal. Solar intermittency is experienced before it is abstractly summarized.

Forecasts turn failure into a decision

The player can see tonight's peak and projected shortage before darkness. This makes a blackout feel connected to prior planning instead of random punishment.

The newspaper creates cadence

Each dawn transforms graphs into a readable story: what went wrong, when it happened, what it cost, and what the grid office recommends next. The first report, for example, records 39% clean power, 98% reliability but 0% at 19:00, +$6,698 net, and the wire/plant/fuel split behind upkeep.

Upgrades create build identity

Choosing one of three structural modifiers changes how the same rules should be approached. Captured picks include Wire Crews (−25% line upkeep), Neighbors on Call (−12% evening demand), and Grid-Forming Inverters (battery discharge rises from 15 to 18 MW).

Where the first session strains

The dashboard asks for expert scanning

Town state, network warnings, forecast, stacked generation chart, pollution, finance, build list, and goal compete simultaneously. The information is strong; its moment-to-moment priority is less clear.

Progress can hide the decisive failure

The Sustainable City percentage rose while the pollution timer approached zero and evening shortages worsened. A rising headline percentage can make the run feel healthier than it is.

Reports explain more than they prescribe

The newspaper names the outage accurately, but the next best action still requires translating a post-mortem into a purchase, site, and timing decision.

Modal cadence interrupts flow

Dawn report, pause state, upgrade draft, and tutorial messaging can stack in quick succession. Each is useful, but together they slow the return from diagnosis to building.

Recommendations

1 · Rank the next risk

Condense the dashboard into one primary warning: “Pollution cap in ~1 day” or “35 MW short at 18:00.” Keep the full charts available beneath that priority.

2 · Turn reports into actions

Attach one-click filters to the diagnosis: highlight unserved homes, reveal candidate battery sites, or preselect the firm-capacity category mentioned by the report.

3 · Show objective dependencies

Break the Sustainable City percentage into explicit gates and identify the blocker. A player should know whether the next bottleneck is homes, reliability, gas, firm capacity, or pollution.

4 · Teach evening capacity earlier

After the first solar panel, ghost the full sunset deficit and let the player compare Gas and Battery outcomes before committing. This is the simulation's central causal lesson.

5 · Compress repeated ceremony

After the first two dawns, offer a compact report with an optional full Gazette. Preserve the fiction while shortening the route back to the town.

6 · Strengthen the daily return

End Today's Grid with a compact share card that exposes the decisive trade-off—clean share, worst shortfall, and one upgrade path—so players can compare strategies, not only scores.

Interface specification

Evidence convention. Observed means the state is visible in the reviewed session or captured UI. Implementation guidance marks a production requirement inferred from the interaction model, not a claim about unseen code.

Viewport map

Town planning map

The central town/grid is the spatial truth: buildings, generation reach, placement sites, and construction ghosts appear over an isometric or plan-style settlement.

System dashboard

Cash, pollution, day/time, tonight forecast, supply-versus-demand, and cash-flow information frame the map along the top/right without hiding the buildable area.

Build, objective, and report layers

A building palette/guide sits on the left or bottom; goals stay visible; daily briefing, newspaper, upgrade draft, and loss use structured modal cards.

Overlays & interruptions

  • Consent, settings, stats, and mode selection before the city view.
  • Today’s Grid scenario briefing and first-solar tutorial coachmark.
  • Dawn newspaper report that joins reliability, profit, pollution, graph, cause, and advice.
  • Three-card Grid Upgrade draft and pollution-cap loss/feedback modal.

Motion, VFX & feedback

  • Build ghost, valid/invalid cell overlay, reach radius, site-quality treatment, and placement snap.
  • Day/night lighting and time-speed motion make the energy cycle visible on the town.
  • Supply/demand lines animate to new projections; MW surplus/shortfall and cash/pollution deltas pulse at their source.
  • Outage, reliability, and pollution warnings escalate before terminal failure without masking the planning surface.
  • Upgrade selection lights affected systems and persists as a compact badge or list entry.

Responsive, accessibility & edge cases

  • Dense charts and map cells need keyboard/list equivalents plus accessible names, values, and units.
  • Use line pattern, labels, icons, and signed values so supply/demand and safe/danger states survive color-vision differences.
  • For narrow screens, prioritize the map and selected building; convert forecast/metrics to swipeable sheets rather than miniature panels.
  • Save only at deterministic planning/report boundaries and prevent dawn, upgrade, or loss from resolving twice after reload.
Reconstruction test. A player should read the day’s objectives, place the tutorial solar asset and a constrained generator, predict tonight’s balance, control time, connect a shortage or surplus to the dawn report, choose one upgrade, and understand exactly why pollution triggers failure.

Creator context · verified public sources

Developer dossier

Who made Grid Town, the public context around the work, and the nearest verified projects. Private identity, location, employment, and credits are left unknown unless the creator or an official project page states them.

Public identity and credit

Grid Town is a personal project by Trevor Hinkle, a full-stack product manager and designer working through his independent Lighthouse practice. His official portfolio directly lists Grid Town among personal lab projects.

Location and working context

Hinkle’s official site says he is based in Amsterdam, Netherlands. His professional focus is energy, climate, and infrastructure software—context that directly aligns with Grid Town’s electricity-system design.

Timeline

Before the game, Hinkle led product and business work at Electricity Maps. Grid Town was publicly shared as a playable browser project in September 2026, alongside current independent consulting and product experiments.

Other verified work

His official site names Braintrust (a Claude Code plugin) and MetroMap as other personal lab projects. Client/project work includes software for World Resources Institute ecosystem restoration, Leap virtual power plants, BuildQ AI due diligence, and GHG Protocol workflows.

Visible development pattern

The work bridges domain expertise and approachable interaction design: dense energy concepts become a daily build/forecast/report loop, with consequences expressed through reliability, cash, and pollution rather than a purely technical grid model.

What this means for the teardown

Developer background is unusually relevant evidence here. The game’s educational clarity and dashboard structure reflect real energy-product work; still, the simulation is a designed game model, not a validated power-system planning tool.

Identity boundary. This dossier uses Hinkle’s own portfolio statements. It does not confuse Lighthouse with similarly named studios or attribute client organizations’ whole products to one contributor.

04
Reconstruction blueprint

What must exist to rebuild the observed game

This is a product and systems specification derived from the public build and the recorded first session. It describes observable behaviour, not the original source-code architecture.

Reconstruction confidence. High for the guided intro, plant portfolio, dashboard, daily cadence, upgrades, and pollution loss. Medium for Historical/Sandbox variants, all challenge modifiers, and long-run balance.

State machineSession flow

  • Mode / challenge briefing → select Today's Grid, Historical, Sandbox, or guided play.
  • Live simulation → hourly demand, generation, storage, cash flow, growth, and pollution advance continuously.
  • Build / inspect / demolish → place sources within terrain and connection rules while time continues unless paused.
  • Evening peak → solar falls away; storage, wind, gas, hydro, or nuclear must cover the shortfall.
  • Dawn report → summarise reliability, clean share, finance, outages, and causal advice.
  • Upgrade draft → choose one of three structural modifiers, then enter the next daily cycle.
  • Terminal state → achieve and hold Sustainable City gates, or lose to pollution / financial failure.

Input contractControls

  • Mouse selects a build category, places plants, inspects assets, and demolishes objects.
  • Number keys 1–6 select generation/storage categories.
  • Space pauses; 1×, 2×, and 3× control simulation speed.
  • Zoom, pan, and camera rotation support spatial planning across the growing town.

Rules engineSimulation and resolution

  • Demand changes by hour and building type; homes, shops, factories, and data centres add different load.
  • Solar is daytime-only, wind varies, gas is dispatchable but polluting, batteries shift surplus, hydro requires river sites, and nuclear is costly firm capacity.
  • Generation and connection are separate: a plant needs output and enough network reach to serve new buildings.
  • Site-quality previews alter output; wire distance and plant operation contribute ongoing cost.
  • Tonight's forecast compares projected demand with available supply before the peak arrives.
  • Sustainable City requires 50 powered homes, overnight reliability, no gas burn, sufficient firm/charged capacity, and 90 seconds of maintained clean operation.
  • Pollution is a hard loss clock; the rules also warn that a negative balance can end the run.

Meta layerEconomy and progression

  • Town growth creates demand and income automatically, so every success enlarges the next capacity problem.
  • Dawn converts the continuous simulation into daily evaluation and an upgrade opportunity.
  • Observed upgrades reduce wire upkeep, lower evening demand, or raise battery discharge, creating different grid identities.
  • Today's Grid wraps the same systems in a named three-day threat and a shared challenge target.

Minimum useful data model

  • BuildingLoad: type, location, hourly demand profile, income, connection status, growth trigger.
  • PlantDefinition: capex, capacity, output curve, fuel cost, emissions, reach, terrain/site multiplier, dispatch rule.
  • BatteryState: capacity, charge, charge/discharge limits, efficiency, connection, upgrade modifiers.
  • GridGraph: sources, loads, wire edges, reach/upkeep calculations, served/unserved allocation each simulation tick.
  • RunState: clock/day, cash ledger, pollution, town seed, objective gates, upgrades, forecasts, daily aggregates.
  • ReportSnapshot: worst outage, reliability, clean share, profit, cost split, chart series, diagnosis, suggested action.

06
Production sequence

Build the causal loop before the content surface

A practical implementation order for reproducing the observed promise while keeping the prototype testable at every step.

  1. Build an hourly load curve and solar/gas supply model with pause and time acceleration.
  2. Add a spatial connection graph, source reach, site validity, and served/unserved homes.
  3. Add wind variability, battery state-of-charge, hydro sites, nuclear, capex, upkeep, fuel, and pollution.
  4. Add growth, nightly forecasting, Sustainable City gates, dawn reports, and one upgrade draft per day.
  5. Validate with deterministic simulation seeds and explicit conservation tests for energy, cash, storage, and emissions.

Boundaries and unresolved behaviour

Do not encode these as facts yet.
  • Historical and Sandbox rules, complete challenge rotation, and all upgrades were not enumerated.
  • The exact dispatch priority, curtailment logic, wire-routing algorithm, and cooling-water penalty formula need implementation-level verification.
  • Long-run town growth, late financial failure, and the successful Sustainable City ending were not reached.
